text:
Saudi Arabia's AI data centre story moved from framework to binding debt this month.

On 9 November, Infra and HUMAIN announced two financing agreements totalling up to SAR 2.5 billion ($667m). They are the first transactions under Infra's AI Data Center Financing Program. They turn just over half of the earlier non-binding framework into binding facilities.

For scale, Alvarez & Marsal estimates that delivering about half of announced Saudi capacity by 2030 would need up to $42 billion of project capital, including $32 billion of debt.

The distance between announced capacity and signed debt is where the structuring happens: offtake, power and construction risk.

headline: Frontier and Emerging markets; Islamic Wealth Management; Islamic Marketing; Сlimate finance; Aviation aficionado
text:
KSA's finance jobs: is the era of the expat financial professional coming to an end?

Saudi Arabia has announced mandatory 50% Saudization across 17 financial professions, effective 23 May 2027.
The targeted positions include investment managers, financial advisers, treasury specialists, credit managers, investment analysts and financial product development specialists.

Meanwhile, separate Saudization requirements for accounting professions are scheduled to reach 70% by October 2028. 

Interestingly, although Saudi Central Bank – SAMA- and Capital Market Authority-supervised activities are exempt from this particular decision, localisation is already well advanced in the regulated financial sector:
- alinma — 96% Saudi employees
- The Saudi Investment Bank — 95.79%
- Capital market institutions — 76%.

Saudi Arabia is becoming increasingly selective about the international expertise it needs.
General financial qualifications and international experience alone may no longer be sufficient.
Specialised expertise in Sukuk structuring, Islamic capital markets, complex project finance, securitisation and cross-border M&A could become increasingly valuable.

#saudiAaabia #saudization #islamicfinance #employment #capitalmarkets #vision2030

author: George Berry
headline: Executive Search at Aventus & Co-Founder of Psyched
text:
There is a lot of noise around Saudi Arabia at the moment.

Some projects are being slowed or reworked, some leadership teams are changing, and the financial pressure is real. The easy version of the story is that the ambition is fading. 

I don’t think that’s quite right.

The more interesting story is that Saudi Arabia is becoming more selective about where the money goes, which projects deserve to survive, and which businesses can start attracting outside capital rather than relying indefinitely on the state.

This represents a harder phase of Vision 2030, but probably a healthier one.

We're still very committed to the market. Aventus opened our Saudi office this year, we continue to work with many major Saudi institutions, and we fully expect to do a lot more there over the coming years.

While some firms are leaving or pulling back, we are still settling in.

That doesn’t mean ignoring the challenges. It means believing the underlying transformation is still very real, even if the next phase looks less spectacular and a lot more disciplined.

And the pressure is becoming increasingly literal: the PIF Tower in Riyadh was hit for the second time in less than a week yesterday, with 11 people injured an extraordinary symbol of the geopolitical disruption now landing directly on the institution at the centre of Saudi Arabia’s economic transformation.

I’ve written a fuller piece on what is changing across Public Investment Fund (PIF), NEOM, New Murabba, leadership, Saudisati

$400 million. And it’s not another startup funding round.

Saudi fintech company Tamara recently announced $400 million in asset-backed financing facilities with MUFG and Standard Chartered.

We’re used to seeing headlines about startups raising millions from investors. But this deal is slightly different, as it involves financing backed by assets rather than raising money by selling equity.

A few things worth highlighting:

~ $200 million equivalent in Saudi riyal-denominated financing from Japan’s MUFG.

~ $200 million added to Tamara’s existing financing facility with Standard Chartered.

~ Tamara now serves over 26 million customers and 160,000 merchants across Saudi Arabia and the GCC.

Tamara has grown into a major player in the region’s fintech market, and securing financing from two international banks is another development worth following.

For someone like me who’s interested in business and strategy, there’s a lot to learn from following how companies grow, finance their operations and build relationships with financial institutions.

author: MOHAMED AZIM
headline: Growth Owner | Business development Consultant | Executive Coach | Ai Strategy & Execution
text:
بعض أعظم قصص النمو في العالم لم تُخترع… بل تم الاستحواذ عليها.
Some of the world's greatest growth stories weren't invented. They were acquired.

Elon Musk didn't found Tesla. He invested in 2004, took the chair and scaled it.
Ray Kroc didn't create McDonald's. He bought it and built an empire.

The Gulf is writing the same story:

• Aramco × SABIC (US$69.1B): a global petrochemicals leader, in one deal
• Almarai: grew from dairy into bakery and poultry through acquisitions
• Savvy Games × Scopely (US$4.9B): a global gaming platform, overnight
• ADNOC/XRG × Covestro (€14.7B): the Gulf's largest European buyout in nearly two decades

في عصر رؤية 2030، السرعة ميزة تنافسية.
M&A buys time, talent and market access in a single move.

But after 15+ years working with leaders across the GCC, I've seen the same pattern:
the deal is signed in months, and the value is lost in the integration.
الصفقة تُوقَّع في أشهر… والقيمة تضيع في الدمج.

The deals that win get four things right:

	1.	A clear strategic reason
	2.	Honest due diligence
	3.	Disciplined valuation
	4.	Integration planned before Day 1

This is the framework I work through with senior leaders in my M&A training. 📸

المستقبل لمن يعرف متى يبني… ومتى يستحوذ.

—

#MergersAndAcquisitions #الاندماج_والاستحواذ #Vision2030 #SaudiArabia #Leadership

author: GCC Business for Sale
headline: 10 followers
text:
Most business owners focus on the pitch deck. The real money is in the messy details.

I was speaking with a founder yesterday who was shocked his deal fell through. His product was great. His margins were solid. But the buyer walked.

Why? His contracts with key suppliers were signed over WhatsApp.

In the GCC market, relationships are built on trust and a handshake. That’s how business gets done. But when you step into the M&A world, international buyers want to see airtight paperwork.

If your corporate documents, financials, and contracts aren’t ready for a microscope, you are leaving money on the table.

Buyers don't just buy potential; they buy verified reality. Before you even think about listing your business, we always recommend a "Readiness Audit."

Are your ducks in a row? Or just in the same pond?

If you're thinking about an exit in 2027, let’s have a confidential chat about what needs fixing before you go to market.

author: Darsh Bherwani
headline: BCom Accounting and Finance at Curtin Dubai | Aspiring ACCA and CFA Candidate | Corporate Finance and Investment Analysis
text:
The M&A Volume-vs-Value Paradox: Why UAE Deal Value Surged While Deal Count Fell
Look at the latest H1 2026 GCC and MENA M&A data, and a striking divergence jumps off the page: total regional transaction volume declined by roughly 18% year-on-year, yet disclosed GCC deal value climbed 12.1% to $65.1 billion—with the UAE capturing 80.9% of total regional value (~$52.6 billion).   
Speak to investment bankers, private equity deal teams, and corporate development heads across Dubai, and the institutional shift behind those numbers is unmistakable:
The Old Volume Playbook: Broad, opportunistic bolt-on dealmaking fueled by cheap liquidity, loose due diligence, and aggressive top-line revenue multiples—where almost any profitable mid-market company could attract multiple bids. 
The High-Conviction Capital Playbook: Fewer transactions, larger check sizes, and ruthless underwriting discipline—where sovereign-backed platforms, strategic consolidators, and DIFC buyout funds deploy massive capital exclusively into category leaders with verified cash conversion, clean IFRS financials, and defensible ROIC.
In 2026, capital hasn’t retreated from the UAE; it has become radically selective. Acquirers are willing to pay premium valuations for scalable, audit-ready platforms—while walking away early from businesses with messy related-party ledgers, unverified EBITDA add-backs, or fragile working capital cycles.

author: Avinash Vashistha
headline: Chairman & CEO, Tholons | Deal Origination and GTM in AI Reinvention & GCC/GBS | Board / CxO AI Advisory | Ex-Chairman & CEO, Accenture (I)
text:
2026 is the year the GCC became a tradable asset.

In eight months: 

Wipro bought Mindsprint (Olam), HCLTech bought Guardian India, TCS bought MHP (Porsche), and TCS took over Best Buy India. 

Today, bp moved ~3,000 finance staff in India, Hungary and Malaysia to Wipro. 

Cognizant is in talks for ~1,500 people in S&P Global's Capital IQ operations.

Now look at what was actually paid:

→ Guardian India: $10.5M for ~2,000 people and ~₹579 crore of revenue. Roughly 0.15x.
→ MHP: €320M on €742M of turnover. About 0.4x.
→ Mindsprint: $375M on $135.6M of revenue. About 2.8x.

Same trend, nearly a 20x spread. Why?

Mindsprint and MHP sold IP, outside clients and domain depth. Guardian sold a captive, and a captive's "revenue" is cost-plus billing to its own parent. On the open market, a pure captive is not an asset. It is a liability transfer with a contract attached.

That's the real story. The buyer is buying the contract, not the centre. Olam committed $800M over eight years. Porsche committed €1.25B over five. Guardian signed for seven. The purchase price is the entry ticket to revenue visibility, at a time when AI is compressing everything else.
